demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Mereana had been 46 when her life split apart in a way that still felt impossible to hold in one piece. She was a forensic analyst in a busy county laboratory, the kind of job that required steady hands, concentration, and a capacity to sit with disturbing evidence without flinching. It had happened on an ordinary evening after work, when her husband rang her from home and, in a few seconds that seemed to stretch and fracture, she heard the sound of him choking, gasping, and then going suddenly quiet. By the time she reached him, he was gone. In the months that followed, Mereana came to experience that death not as a finished event but as a sequence of frozen images: the phone in her hand, the sound in the receiver, his body on the floor. She described the memory as only a few moments, each one like a picture that appeared too sharply, as if lit from inside. At the worst times, when the memory forced its way back, she would also hear the sounds she had heard that night in her head, especially the choking and the abrupt silence, and the flood of emotion would become so intense that she had to stop whatever she was doing.

From the beginning, Mereana's understanding of what had happened was shaped by devastation and betrayal. She had lost faith in people, in life, and in any higher power she once assumed would make suffering make sense. She spoke with flat certainty that her life had been destroyed by the trauma, and that nothing in it felt meaningful anymore. Those beliefs were not abstract to her; they shaped her days. Work, which had once given her structure and a sense of competence, now felt like an arena she had to force herself into. On the mornings when she was supposed to go in, she would sit in the dark kitchen and stare at her uniform, telling herself that she could not face other people, ordinary conversation, or the sight of her own reflection in the staff bathroom. She began avoiding work whenever she could, taking sick leave, arriving late, and making excuses that sounded plausible to colleagues. At home, she stayed up until very late because the idea of sleep felt like surrendering to the hours when the images came most easily. She ate little, sometimes restricting food entirely, because hunger seemed more manageable than the sick heaviness in her stomach and the sense that she did not deserve comfort. Over time, these habits became part of the way she tried to survive what she believed life had become.

Yet the very strategies that gave her temporary relief deepened the meanings she attached to the loss. Each morning she managed not to go to work, she felt more certain that nothing meaningful remained for her and that the life she had known really was over. The empty hours at night and the days when she barely ate left her more drained and more alone, and that exhaustion made the world feel even less trustworthy and less alive. At work, when she did manage to appear, the lab itself became a place where memory could ambush her. A phone ringing sharply in another office, a colleague's cough cut off mid-breath, or the sudden hush after a door closed could bring back the sounds from that night with force. When that happened, the memories came not as a story but as fragments: a picture of the phone, a picture of the hallway, a picture of her husband's body, accompanied by the internal replay of those frightening sounds. Because she was already so depleted from staying up late, avoiding food, and dragging herself through work when she did go, she had less capacity to steady herself; the memory would overwhelm her faster, and she would have to stop, sit down, or leave the room. The more often that happened, the more convinced she became that her life had been permanently damaged and that she could no longer trust herself to function.

By the time she sought help, Mereana was living in a narrow and punishing rhythm. She pushed herself to keep some parts of work going because the lab was also the place where bills were paid and appearances were maintained, but every shift felt threatened by the possibility of hearing something that would send her back to that night. She avoided eating through much of the day, stayed awake until the house was silent, and then lay in bed fearing sleep and the return of the images. What finally brought her to therapy was the realization that the pattern was tightening rather than easing: the more she withdrew from work, sleep, and food, the more meaningless and ruined her life felt, and the more power the memories seemed to have over her. She came because she was frightened that she was disappearing into the aftermath of his death, and because despite everything she still hoped there might be some way to live without feeling that the world had ended with him.
